1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.c4.strategy: Attacks the d5 pawn straight away. If Black takes on c4 the pawn offer is only temporary; otherwise White keeps the tension and presses for a lasting space advantage in the centre. The most direct way to fight for the centre, and the reason this is the main line.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bf4.name: Queen's Pawn Game: London System
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bf4.background: James Mason, an Irish-American, was the first master-level player to use the London System regularly, including at the strong Vienna tournament of 1882. Its name comes from the London tournament of 1922, where it appeared seven times, in games by Capablanca, Alekhine and Rubinstein among others. In the 21st century it has become popular among club players for its solid nature and clear plans.
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bf4.strategy: Brings the dark-squared bishop outside the pawn chain before e3 can shut it in, with a knight on e5 as the central outpost in view. The set-up is solid and needs little theory, but with the bishop gone from c1 the b2 pawn has no defender, which Black's queen can target.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bg5.strategy: Pressures the f6 knight and develops outside the pawn chain, aiming at quick, harmonious development and a kingside attack rather than an early fight for space. The set-up gives White little more than equality, but it is calm, easy to learn and rich in practical chances.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3.background: Popularised in the 1920s by the Belgian master Edgard Colle and developed further by George Koltanowski. Reference works describe it as unfashionable in master play.
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3.strategy: Builds a compact centre and prepares the central break e4, for which the minor pieces are brought into place first. The cost is passivity: the dark-squared bishop stays shut in behind the e3 pawn, and Black can choose a set-up freely without much to fear.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.g3.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Symmetrical Variation, Pseudo-Catalan
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.g3.strategy: Prepares a fianchetto so the bishop can press on d5 and the long diagonal, but plays it before the c-pawn has challenged d5. Black can bring the light-squared bishop out on its own terms and equalises without trouble, so the move order is less accurate than the others.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bf4 c5.strategy: Strikes at d4 at once, trying to take space and open the game before White's solid set-up is ready. The bishop has left c1, so b2 is without a defender, and Black's counterplay often starts there. Black takes the initiative instead of waiting.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bf4 e6.strategy: Supports d5 and opens the diagonal of the king's bishop, a solid set-up that mirrors White's own. Black does not strike at the centre at once and the c8 bishop is shut in behind the pawn chain, but the position is sound and Black can still challenge the centre later.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bf4 Bf5.strategy: Develops the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain before the e-pawn moves, mirroring White's own bishop. A sound, symmetrical set-up that tends to be drawish; a knight move to h4 attacks the bishop, so Black has to know where it retreats.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bf4 c5 4.e3.name: Queen's Pawn Game: London System
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bf4 c5 4.e3.strategy: Defends d4 with a pawn and opens a diagonal for the king's bishop; because the bishop on f4 is already outside the chain, it is not shut in. White keeps a solid centre and a quiet game, but b2 still has no defender and has to be watched.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bf4 c5 4.c3.strategy: Supports d4 with a pawn, but does not cover b2, so a queen move to b6 makes White react at once, and the pawn takes the best square from the queen's knight. A solid but slower build-up than the e-pawn, which also opens the bishop's diagonal.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bf4 c5 4.dxc5.strategy: Takes the pawn and releases the central tension, but Black can win it back with a developing move and White has given up the d4 pawn that held the centre. The solid set-up is gone and Black gets the freer game.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bf4 c5 4.e3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece and adds a second attacker on d4, keeping the pressure on the centre while the queen stays at home. The tension on d4 stays, Black keeps all its central pawn breaks in hand, and the queen is not exposed to harassment.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bf4 c5 4.e3 Qb6.strategy: Hits the b2 pawn, which the bishop left undefended, and makes White react before settling in. The price is an early queen sortie: Black spends time on it while its pieces are still at home, so it pays only if the pressure on b2 stays uncomfortable.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bf4 c5 4.e3 cxd4.strategy: Opens the centre at once: after the recapture Black has a half-open c-file and an easy game, but gives up the pressure on d4 and leaves White a firm pawn centre. A quiet, level position in which neither side has many chances to unbalance it.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bf4 c5 4.e3 Nc6 5.Nb.name: Queen's Pawn Game: London System
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bf4 c5 4.e3 Nc6 5.Nb.background: Ding Liren played it with White against Ian Nepomniachtchi in game 6 of the 2023 World Chess Championship and won.
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bf4 c5 4.e3 Nc6 5.Nb.strategy: Develops the last minor piece without committing the c-pawn. The knight covers e4 and b3, and White keeps a flexible, solid set-up in which d4 stays defended by the e3 pawn and the f3 knight.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bf4 c5 4.e3 Nc6 5.c3.strategy: Gives d4 a second pawn defender, but it does not cover b2 and takes the c3 square from the queen's knight, so ...Qb6 forces White to trade queens or find a defence at once. A solid idea that costs time against the sharpest reply.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bf4 c5 4.e3 Nc6 5.Nc.strategy: Develops the knight to the centre, where it adds pressure on d5, but it blocks the c-pawn and leaves b2 without protection, so Black's queen can go for it at once. White gives up the standard solid set-up for quicker piece play.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bf4 c5 4.e3 Nc6 5.Nb.strategy: Supports d5 with a pawn and opens the diagonal of the king's bishop, building the sturdy centre this set-up wants while the tension on d4 stays. The cost is a light-squared bishop shut in behind its own pawns, which Black has to free later.

Settles the tension in the centre at once. After White recaptures, Black has a half-open c-file and can bring the light-squared bishop out before closing it in with the e-pawn. A comfortable, balanced game in which Black's pieces develop easily.
Goes for b2, the pawn the bishop's move left undefended, and makes White deal with it at once. The queen leaves home early, so the sortie pays only if the pressure on b2 keeps costing White time.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bf4 c5 4.e3 Nc6 5.Nb.name: Queen's Pawn Game: London System
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bf4 c5 4.e3 Nc6 5.Nb.strategy: Gives d4 a second pawn defender and takes b4 away from Black's knight, completing White's standard pawn structure. White commits to a closed, slow game in which the pieces gather behind the pawns and the aim is a knight on e5.

Brings the bishop to the diagonal toward h7 and prepares e4 without first playing c3. It leaves d4 with fewer defenders: Black can exchange in the centre, and a knight jump to b4 then attacks the bishop with tempo.

Takes on c5 and releases the tension, but Black wins the pawn back with a developing move and White has given up the d4 pawn that held the centre. White's solid set-up is gone and Black gets the freer game.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bf4 c5 4.e3 Qb6 5.Nc.name: London System: Poisoned Pawn Variation
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bf4 c5 4.e3 Qb6 5.Nc.strategy: Develops with a point and leaves b2 en prise on purpose: after ...Qxb2 the knight jumps to b5 and threatens Nc7+, forking king and rook, while the queen is far from home. If Black declines, White has developed with a gain of time. The sharpest, most principled answer to the queen sortie.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bf4 c5 4.e3 Qb6 5.Nb.strategy: Offers b2 as well while developing the second knight. If Black takes, the rook attacks the queen at once and White develops with tempo, but without a knight on c3 there is no Nb5 threat, so Black can accept more calmly.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.Bf4 c5 4.e3 Qb6 5.Qc.strategy: Defends b2 and avoids all sharpness, but the queen stands passively on c1. White gives Black time to finish development or to gain queenside space, so it is a safe but second-rate answer to the queen sortie.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.c4 e6.strategy: Holds d5 with a pawn instead of taking on c4, keeping the centre closed and the structure sound. The cost is a light-squared bishop that stays shut in behind its own pawns for a while: a slightly passive but very solid game.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.c4 c6.strategy: Also holds d5 with a pawn, but keeps the diagonal of the light-squared bishop open, so it can develop outside the pawn chain. A solid choice with a clear plan; the cost is that the queen's knight loses its natural square on c6.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.c4 b5.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Zilbermints Countergambit
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.c4 b5.strategy: A countergambit: Black offers a pawn to deflect White's c-pawn and open the queenside. But White can simply take it with cxb5, and Black has nothing concrete to show for the pawn except a weakened queenside.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 e6.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 e6.strategy: The most natural reply: Black supports d5, opens the king's bishop and keeps every later set-up open. White's quiet pieces do not threaten anything yet, so Black can choose freely; the cost is a light-squared bishop that is shut in behind the pawns.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 Bf5.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Anti-Colle
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 Bf5.strategy: Develops the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain before a pawn can shut it in, and makes it hard for White's bishop to reach d3, since it would be traded at once. White's plan rests on that bishop and the e4 break, so White has to change course.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 g6.strategy: Prepares a fianchetto, so the bishop will press on d4 along the long diagonal instead of mirroring White's set-up. Sound but slower: Black still has to find a plan for the centre, while White carries on with the planned bishop move and the e4 break.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 e6 4.Bd3.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 e6 4.Bd3.strategy: Puts the bishop on the diagonal toward h7 and aims for the e4 break, the heart of the set-up. The dark-squared bishop stays passive behind e3 for now, which is the price of White's compact structure.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 e6 4.b3.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 e6 4.b3.background: The Colle-Zukertort System, which develops the dark-squared bishop on b2, is named after Johannes Zukertort. Artur Yusupov often played it at grandmaster level.
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 e6 4.b3.strategy: Gives the dark-squared bishop an active post on b2 instead of leaving it passive behind e3, and supports a later c4. White trades the solid c3 set-up for more active piece play on the long diagonal, with a kingside attack in view.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 e6 4.c4.strategy: Strikes at d5 at once instead of waiting for the slow build-up. White gives up the compact set-up and its e4 break for an ordinary fight over central space, with the pawn on e3 solidly behind d4. Sound, but White now has to know the usual queen's-pawn middlegames.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 e6 4.b3 c5.strategy: Challenges d4 at once, before White's bishop reaches b2, and claims central space. A natural counter that makes White decide how to hold the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 e6 4.b3 Bd6.strategy: Develops the bishop on the diagonal that takes e5 and eyes h2, and prepares castling. Black builds a set-up that mirrors White's, but has to keep an eye on White's e4 break.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 e6 4.b3 b6.strategy: Answers White's plan in kind: the queen's bishop goes to b7, where it fights for e4 and the long diagonal. A compact, symmetrical position, though slower than striking at d4 at once, and it leaves White the choice of how to build up.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 e6 4.b3 c5 5.Bb2.strategy: Develops the bishop on the long diagonal, where it backs up d4 and, once the centre opens, points at Black's kingside. White gets an active bishop without having to play c3.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 e6 4.b3 c5 5.Bd3.strategy: Develops the king's bishop on its attacking diagonal toward h7 and prepares to castle, leaving White free to place the other bishop on b2 at the right moment. If Black takes on d4, the recapture with the e-pawn gives White a half-open e-file and a firm centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 e6 4.b3 c5 5.Nbd2.strategy: Brings the second knight to d2, where it guards the knight on f3 and backs a later e4, and leaves the king's bishop free to choose its square. A sound, flexible development, though less direct in putting pressure on Black than a bishop move.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 e6 4.b3 c5 5.Bb2.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 e6 4.b3 c5 5.Bb2.background: The Colle–Zukertort System, characterised by developing the dark-squared bishop on b2, is named after Johannes Zukertort, and Artur Yusupov has frequently played it at grandmaster level.
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 e6 4.b3 c5 5.Bb2.strategy: Brings a second piece to bear on d4, the pawn White's whole set-up rests on, and keeps Black's development simple. White has to keep d4 well guarded before pushing on with the central break, and Black's pieces stay free to castle and fight for the centre.
Defends the c5 pawn that White's d4 pawn attacks, and the bishop takes e5 and eyes h2. Black develops with a purpose and prepares to castle, but has to watch White's e4 break.

Develops the queen's bishop on b7 to challenge White's on the long diagonal, and fights for e4. Solid, but it leaves the tension on d4 as it is, so White can resolve it by taking on c5 and open the diagonal of the b2 bishop toward f6.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 e6 4.b3 c5 5.Bb2.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 e6 4.b3 c5 5.Bb2.strategy: Puts the bishop on its natural diagonal, aimed at Black's kingside, and clears the way to castling. It completes the compact set-up the system is built for: solid pawns on d4 and e3, pieces ready to support the central break and, if Black is careless, a kingside attack.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 e6 4.b3 c5 5.Bb2.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 e6 4.b3 c5 5.Bb2.strategy: Develops the last knight to a square where it protects f3 and backs the central break. It is a sound alternative, but it leaves the king's bishop undecided and the king uncastled, so it is a little less direct than putting the bishop out first.

Releases the tension and opens the long diagonal for the bishop on b2, but Black regains the pawn at once with the bishop. White has then given up the d4 pawn the whole set-up rests on, and Black's bishop stands actively on c5, pressing on e3.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 e6 4.Bd3 Bd6.strategy: Develops the bishop to the diagonal where it controls e5 and aims at h2, ahead of castling. Black builds a solid set-up that mirrors White's. The price is a bishop on a square that White's central break can later hit, so that break is the thing to watch.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 e6 4.Bd3 c5.strategy: Challenges d4 at once, the pawn the whole set-up rests on, before White has settled which pieces support it. Black claims space and a share of the initiative, and White has to choose between keeping d4 guarded and resolving the tension.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 e6 4.Bd3 b6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the queen's bishop, from where it fights for e4, the square White's whole set-up depends on, at a distance. Black accepts a slower start in return for a flexible structure and pressure against the central break.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 e6 4.Bd3 Nbd7.strategy: A compact development that supports e5 and keeps the c-pawn free. It is passive, though: the knight does not fight for e4 and the light-squared bishop stays shut in behind e6, so White gets time to carry out its central break at leisure.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 e6 4.Bd3 Bd6 5.O-.strategy: Gets the king safe before the centre is settled, while the bishop on d3 and the knight on f3 keep their eyes on Black's kingside. White still has every set-up open and chooses later how the queenside pieces come out.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 e6 4.Bd3 Bd6 5.Nb.strategy: Develops the last knight to the square from which it backs the e4 break together with the bishop on d3. White keeps its play compact and solid, at the price of a dark-squared bishop that stays passive behind its own pawns.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 e6 4.Bd3 Bd6 5.c3.strategy: Supports d4 with a pawn and builds a compact centre ready for e4. The price is that the dark-squared bishop has no good diagonal, and White commits to the traditional plan rather than the fianchetto.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 e6 4.Bd3 Bd6 5.O-.strategy: Mirrors White and castles. The h7 pawn is the target of the bishop on d3, but the king and the knight on f6 cover it well. With the king safe, Black can concentrate on the fight for e4 and e5, where the game will be decided.

Challenges d4 at once and claims a share of the centre while White's pieces are unsettled. White must decide how to keep d4 guarded, and Black has to be ready for a fight in the middle, with the bishop on d6 placed to recapture on c5.

Brings the queenside knight to a flexible square, where it supports a pawn break in the centre and leaves the c-pawn free to strike at d4. The cost is passivity: the knight does not fight for e4, and the light-squared bishop, shut in behind e6, still has to find a route out.

Prepares to develop the queen's bishop on the long diagonal, where it supports the central break instead of sitting behind the e3 pawn. A patient, flexible plan: the b-pawn also backs a later c4. The bishop stays behind its own d4 pawn until the centre opens.

Develops the last knight to the square from which, with the bishop on d3, it supports the e4 break that is the plan of the whole set-up. White keeps a solid centre and decides later how to arrange the queen's bishop.

Reinforces d4 and builds a compact pawn centre that stands ready for e4. White chooses solidity over activity: the dark-squared bishop stays passive behind its own pawns, but the structure is hard to attack.

Develops the queenside knight so that it supports a central pawn break, keeping the c-pawn free. The cost is that the knight shuts in the light-squared bishop, which has to find another route out, so Black's development stays a little passive.
Hits d4 at once, before the bishop reaches b2 to back it up. Black claims central space and makes White decide how to hold the centre, while the bishop on d6 stands ready to recapture on c5.

Matches White's plan: the queen's bishop goes to b7, where it fights for e4 and the long diagonal. Black gets a compact, symmetrical position and a clear aim, while the c-pawn stays free to strike at d4 when the moment is right.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 g6 4.Bd3.strategy: Keeps to the usual plan against the fianchetto: bishop out, castle, then expand in the centre. Black's bishop will press on d4 along the long diagonal once the knight has moved, so White has to keep that pawn well supported.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 g6 4.c4.strategy: Strikes at d5 straight away instead of waiting for the slow build-up, with e3 solidly behind d4. White plays for space in the centre against the fianchetto, giving up the calm plan of a well-timed e4 for a fight where Black's bishop on g7 will target d4.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 g6 4.b3.strategy: Prepares the queen's bishop for b2, where it backs d4 and faces Black's fianchetto bishop along the long diagonal. White accepts slower development in return for a bishop that is active instead of hemmed in by its own pawn on e3.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 g6 4.Bd3 Bg7.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Colle System, Grünfeld Formation
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 g6 4.Bd3 Bg7.strategy: Completes the fianchetto and prepares castling. The bishop's diagonal towards d4 is for now blocked by its own knight on f6, but it will bear on the centre as soon as the knight moves. Black gets a sound, flexible set-up built on piece pressure rather than pawns.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 g6 4.Bd3 c5.strategy: Attacks d4 at once, before White has had time to reinforce it, and gives the fianchetto bishop something to aim at. If White takes on c5, Black regains the pawn with a check from the queen.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.e3 g6 4.Bd3 Bg4.strategy: Develops the light-squared bishop outside the pawn chain and pins the knight on f3 against the queen. White can drive the bishop off, though, and Black's pieces are not yet coordinated in the centre, so the pin brings little lasting pressure.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.g3 c6.strategy: Supports the d5 pawn with a solid pawn chain, so that White cannot undermine it, and keeps the light-squared bishop free to leave the chain before the e-pawn locks it in. The price is some central flexibility, since the c-pawn is now tied to the defence of d5.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.g3 Bf5.strategy: Takes the light-squared bishop out of the pawn chain before it can be shut in, the main point of meeting g3 at once. The bishop eyes the c2 pawn and the queenside, though White's knight can harass it from h4.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.g3 g6.strategy: Mirrors White's set-up with a fianchetto of its own, so that the bishop on g7 will press on d4 once the knight has moved. Sound, but it does nothing about the light-squared bishop, and White's bishop arrives on g2 with pressure on d5.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.g3 c6 4.Bg2.strategy: The point of the fianchetto: the bishop goes behind the knight on f3, on the long diagonal, where it will press on d5 and the queenside once the knight moves, and White can castle at once. White fights for the centre from a distance and without early pawn commitments.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.g3 c6 4.c4.strategy: Hits d5 at once and fights for the centre, with the fianchetto still to come. White opens the position for the pieces; if Black accepts the pawn, White has to regain it by piece play, so the move asks for precise handling.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.g3 c6 4.Bf4.strategy: Gets the dark-squared bishop out of the pawn chain on an active diagonal before it can be shut in, but delays the king's bishop and sets no clear plan against Black's centre. A sound, harmless set-up that keeps the pawn structure flexible.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.g3 c6 4.Bg2 Bg4.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Symmetrical Variation, Pseudo-Catalan
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.g3 c6 4.Bg2 Bg4.strategy: Develops the bishop outside the pawn chain before ...e6 can shut it in, and pressures the knight on f3 that guards the centre. If Black trades it, White recaptures with the bishop and has the two bishops against the removal of a defender.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.g3 c6 4.Bg2 Bf5.strategy: The point of the pawn on c6: the bishop leaves the chain before ...e6 can lock it in, and from f5 it fights for e4 and eyes the queenside. Black reaches a solid set-up with equal chances while White must still find a plan against the centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.g3 c6 4.Bg2 e6.strategy: Solid but passive: a second pawn supports d5 and the kingside pieces can develop, but the light-squared bishop is shut in behind its own pawns. Black accepts a cramped structure to keep a sound centre.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.g3 c6 4.Bg2 Bg4 5.O-.strategy: Castles at once. The knight on f3 is guarded by the e-pawn and the bishop, so a trade on f3 costs White nothing structurally, and the king is safe behind the fianchettoed bishop before the centre opens.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.g3 c6 4.Bg2 Bg4 5.Ne.strategy: Attacks the bishop at once and puts the knight on the strong e5 square, supported by the d4 pawn. Black must spend time moving the bishop again while White gains central space; nothing is lost on e2, which the queen covers.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.g3 c6 4.Bg2 Bg4 5.h3.strategy: Puts the question to the bishop. A trade on f3 gives White the two bishops; a retreat leaves the pawn on h3 as a slight loosening of the castled king's cover. Sound, but it spends a move on a pawn instead of castling.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.g3 c6 4.Bg2 Bg4 5.O-.name: Queen's Pawn Game: Symmetrical Variation, Pseudo-Catalan
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.g3 c6 4.Bg2 Bg4 5.O-.strategy: Props up d5 with a solid chain and frees the king's bishop. Black gives up the ...e5 break, and the bishop on g4 can be challenged by h3, so Black has to decide soon whether to keep it or trade it for the knight.

Develops the knight to support the centre and keeps the e-pawn flexible, leaving open whether it goes to e6 or e5. The cost is that the king's bishop stays undeveloped for now, and White will challenge d5 at once.

Retreats the bishop to the outside of the pawn chain, where h3 no longer troubles it and it keeps watch over e4. The solid set-up Black is aiming for, but the bishop has spent two moves to get here, so White is a tempo to the good and can start the central play first.

Trades the bishop for the knight before h3 can chase it, but White recaptures with the bishop, which then eyes the d5 pawn and the long diagonal. Black gives up the bishop pair without gaining a tempo and has to defend a slightly cramped position.

1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.g3 c6 4.Bg2 Bg4 5.O-.name: Slav Defence: Modern Line
1.d4 Nf6 2.Nf3 d5 3.g3 c6 4.Bg2 Bg4 5.O-.strategy: Challenges d5, the heart of Black's centre, with the bishop on g2 lined up behind the knight on f3. White gets a game of space and pressure on the queenside, with the knight on f3 well enough guarded to ignore the bishop on g4.

Puts the question to the bishop at once: it must leave its attack on f3 or be exchanged for the knight, which gives White the bishop pair. Otherwise White gains kingside space, at the price of a slightly loosened kingside, a fair trade in a quiet position.

Develops the last minor piece and adds a third defender to the knight on f3, so the bishop on g4 is no bother. A flexible, quiet set-up, but it asks Black no question about d5, and Black can build the centre at leisure.

The calm way to meet the pressure on d5: the c6-d5-e6 chain is solid and the king's bishop is freed. Black accepts a slightly cramped position, with the bishop on g4 still to be settled, in return for a position with no weaknesses.

Exchanges the bishop for the knight that guards d4 and e5, but White recaptures with the bishop, which then bears on d5 and the long diagonal. Black gives up the bishop pair and has to meet the pressure on the centre without that bishop.
Takes the pawn and lets the tension in the centre go, but the extra pawn is hard to hold: White can attack it at once, and Black has given up the d5 pawn that held the centre.
